title: Nearly Half of Adults Over 65 Actually Got Sharper With Age — and Their Mindset Was the Key
excerpt: A Yale study tracking 11,000 Americans for 12 years found that positive beliefs about aging predicted real improvements in cognition and physical function — not just slower decline
body:
The dominant narrative about aging is bleak: after 65, the body weakens, the mind dulls, and decline is inevitable. A sweeping new study from Yale University is challenging that story with data that is hard to dismiss.

Researchers tracked more than 11,000 Americans aged 65 and older for up to 12 years, measuring both cognitive function and physical health at regular intervals. Their finding: 45% of participants actually improved in cognition, walking speed, or both over that period.

That is not a misprint. Nearly half the older adults in a nationally representative study got measurably better at thinking or moving — or both — as they aged.

The Numbers Behind the Surprise

The study, published in the journal *Geriatrics*, drew on data from the Health and Retirement Study, a federally supported longitudinal survey. Researchers assessed cognition through a global performance test (short-term memory, mathematical ability, and related measures) and physical function through walking speed, which geriatricians consider a "vital sign" because of its strong links to disability, hospitalisation, and mortality.

About 32% of participants improved cognitively, 28% improved physically, and many experienced gains that exceeded thresholds considered clinically meaningful. When those whose cognitive scores remained stable — rather than declining — were included, more than half defied the stereotype of inevitable deterioration.

"What's striking is that these gains disappear when you only look at averages," said lead author Becca R. Levy, a professor at the Yale School of Public Health. "If you average everyone together, you see decline. But when you look at individual trajectories, you uncover a very different story."

> ""What's striking is that these gains disappear when you only look at averages," said lead author Becca R."

Why Mindset Matters More Than You Think

The researchers then asked a provocative question: what separated the improvers from the decliners?

The most powerful predictor wasn't wealth, education, or the absence of chronic disease. It was how participants felt about aging itself.

Those who held positive beliefs about getting older — who disagreed with statements like "the older I get, the more useless I feel" and agreed with "I am as happy now as when I was younger" — were significantly more likely to show real improvements in both cognition and walking speed.

This held true even after the researchers controlled for age, sex, education, depression, chronic conditions, and length of follow-up.

The finding builds on Levy's broader research into "stereotype embodiment theory," which argues that age stereotypes absorbed from culture — through social media, advertisements, casual conversation — eventually become biologically consequential. Her prior work has linked negative age beliefs to worse memory, slower walking speed, higher cardiovascular risk, and even biomarkers associated with Alzheimer's disease.

The Cultural Dimension

The study's implications resonate differently across cultures. In Indian tradition, elders are accorded respect and their wisdom is valued — an ethos captured in the Sanskrit concept of *vriddhashram* (eldercare) and the cultural reverence for experience.

But the diaspora experience often introduces a painful tension. NRIs in the US, UK, and Canada frequently watch their parents age from thousands of miles away, absorbing Western narratives of inevitable decline that can shape how they think about — and interact with — their ageing parents.

Levy's research suggests that these cultural narratives are not just attitudes. They are, measurably, health outcomes. The way a family talks about an ageing parent's capabilities may literally influence whether that parent improves or declines.

"Our findings suggest there is often a reserve capacity for improvement in later life," Levy said. "And because age beliefs are modifiable, this opens the door to interventions at both the individual and societal level."

What Can Be Done

The improvements were not confined to people recovering from illness. Even among participants who started with normal cognitive and physical function, a substantial proportion got better — challenging the idea that gains only reflect rebounds from prior setbacks.

The authors hope the findings will reverse the popular perception that continuous decline is inevitable and push policymakers toward more investment in preventive care, rehabilitation, and health-promoting programmes for older adults.

For diaspora families, the takeaway is practical: the conversations you have with ageing parents about their capabilities may matter as much as the medicines they take. Encouragement, engagement, and the cultural refusal to write off older adults are not just kindness — they appear to be, quite literally, medicine.

Sources: *Geriatrics* (2026), DOI: 10.3390/geriatrics11020028; MedicalXpress; Medscape
